meta.purpose: Running out of fuel or charge, and recovering: each club's fuel delivery, EV help, fuel cans and their legal limits, wait times
meta.method: WebSearch for discovery, then WebFetch of each club's own terms or benefit pages. Four PDFs (AAA Northeast terms, the Automobile Club of Southern California member guide, the AA terms booklet, the RAC policy booklet) were saved and their text extracted locally with pypdf, so those quotes are exact apart from line breaks and the PDF's stray spaces before punctuation. Ordinary web pages were read through WebFetch, which returns a model-written extract; a sentence it returned in quotation marks is marked readDetail 'fetch-quote' and was not compared with the raw HTML. Anything resting only on a search engine's summary is marked readMethod 'search-summary' (all of BCAA, because bcaa.com returned 403 to every fetch). Where a figure is computed here by arithmetic it is marked derived and the inputs are given. null means nothing was found; nothing was estimated. The session's WebSearch cap (200) was reached part-way through, so some items below were found by fetching pages directly and some were not found at all; those are listed in notFound.

readDetailKey.pdf-text: document downloaded, text extracted locally; quote exact apart from line breaks and PDF spacing
readDetailKey.fetch-quote: page fetched; the extractor returned the sentence in quotation marks
readDetailKey.search-summary: search engine's summary of the page; the page itself was not read
readDetailKey.carried-over: taken from an earlier file in this folder (research-roadside.json); not re-read today

meta.countsAsCallRule: countsAsCall is true or false only where a source says so about fuel delivery. Where a club lists fuel delivery among its services and caps 'service calls' without naming fuel, it is null and the reasoning is in countsAsCallNote.

containerRules.rule: Petrol may be dispensed at a petrol station into 'a suitable portable container' (reg 12(1)(b)). A container is suitable if it meets Schedule 3 or is an older design that met the 1929 or 1982 rules (Sch 2 para 6). Schedule 3: nominal capacity no greater than 10 litres if plastic, no greater than 20 litres if metal, marked 'PETROL' and 'HIGHLY FLAMMABLE'. Regulation 12 itself sets no number of containers; the keeping limit is 30 litres in total, and in a vehicle no more than two containers (Sch 2 para 1(a)). The Regulations are marked E+W+S (England, Wales, Scotland); Northern Ireland has its own.
containerRules.quote: A portable petrol storage container must— (a) have a nominal capacity — (i) no greater than 10 litres if made of plastic; and (ii) no greater than 20 litres if made of metal;
quoteAlso: 12.—(1) No person is to dispense, or allow the dispensing of, petrol from a dispenser on dispensing premises except— (a) for use in a motor vehicle or motor boat; (b) to fill a suitable portable container or a demountable fuel tank; or (c) for the purpose of maintenance or calibration of the dispenser.
(iii) no more than 30 litres is kept in no more than two suitable portable containers in any motor vehicle, motor boat, hovercraft or aircraft; (Schedule 2 paragraph 1(a))
containerRules.readDetail: fetch-quote (legislation.gov.uk text returned in full; Schedule 3 paragraph 1 fetched twice with the same wording)

containerRules.rule: Consumer portable fuel containers sold in the US must meet the CPSC rule: 16 CFR 1461.2 covers a container 'with a capacity of 5 gallons or less' (18.9 L, derived) and 1461.3 requires ASTM F3326-21 for empty containers (or a safety can meeting section 18 of ANSI/CAN/UL/ULC 30:2022). This is a standard for the can, not a limit on what a station will fill. EPA's definition (40 CFR 59.680) is 'a reusable container of any color that is designed and marketed or otherwise intended for use by consumers for receiving, transporting, storing, and dispensing gasoline, diesel fuel, or kerosene', and all red, yellow or blue utility jugs are deemed portable fuel containers.
containerRules.quote: In accordance with the Portable Fuel Container Safety Act of 2020 (PFCSA), portable fuel containers must comply with the requirements specified in § 1461.3, which are considered to be consumer product safety rules.
quoteAlso: Portable fuel containers sold empty to the consumer must meet the requirements of ASTM F3326-21 (16 CFR 1461.3)

a reusable container of any color that is designed and marketed or otherwise intended for use by consumers for receiving, transporting, storing, and dispensing gasoline, diesel fuel, or kerosene. (40 CFR 59.680)
containerRules.readDetail: fetch-quote (Cornell LII; sections 1461.1 and 59.680 returned whole, 1461.2 and 1461.3 as quoted extracts)

containerRules.rule: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.106 is an employer rule, not a consumer one, but it is the federal definition of an approved flammable-liquid container: 'Only approved containers and portable tanks shall be used', and a safety can is 'an approved container, of not more than 5 gallons capacity'.
containerRules.quote: Safety can shall mean an approved container, of not more than 5 gallons capacity, having a spring-closing lid and spout cover and so designed that it will safely relieve internal pressure when subjected to fire exposure.

containerRules.rule: Sale rule for the can, enforced by the Air Resources Board: a portable fuel container is 'any container or vessel with a nominal capacity of ten gallons or less' (37.9 L, derived) and every portable fuel container system sold in California must be certified through the Air Resources Board; since 1 July 2018 manufacturers cannot sell containers unless certified to CP-501. No limit on what a station will fill was read.
containerRules.quote: any container or vessel with a nominal capacity of ten gallons or less intended for reuse that is designed, used, sold, advertised, or offered for sale for receiving, transporting, storing, and dispensing fuel or kerosene
quoteAlso: Every portable fuel container system manufactured for sale or introduced into California commerce must be 'certified for use and sale by the manufacturer through the Air Resources Board' (13 CCR 2467.2, as summarised by the fetch extractor).
containerRules.sourceDate: Cal. Code Regs. tit. 13, sections 2467.1 and 2467.2

containerRules.rule: Sale rule for the can, 6 NYCRR Part 239 'Portable Fuel Container Spillage Control': a portable fuel container is 'any container or vessel with a nominal capacity of 10 gallons or less' (37.9 L, derived), and since 1 September 2009 none may be sold or supplied in New York unless it complies with 40 CFR 59.653 (the spill-proof system). No New York limit on what a station will fill was read; the NYS and NYC fire codes were not reachable.
containerRules.quote: no person shall import, sell, supply, advertise for sale, offer for sale, or manufacture for sale in the State of New York on or after September 1, 2009, any portable fuel container, spout, or both fuel container and spout which does not comply with 40 CFR section 59.653.
quoteAlso: any container or vessel with a nominal capacity of 10 gallons or less intended for reuse that is designed, used, sold, advertised or offered for sale for receiving, transporting, storing, and dispensing fuel or kerosene. (6 NYCRR 239-2.1)

containerRules.rule: The safety regulator's public guidance (TSSA, on safetyinfo.ca) says to use a certified container and gives handling rules, but no litre limit and no standard by name (CSA B376 and ULC were not mentioned on the page read).
containerRules.quote: Only use a container that has been certified by an accredited certification organization to carry or store fuel.
quoteAlso: When filling a portable container, keep it on the ground with the nozzle in full contact with it.
Fill your container to about 90 percent of its capacity to leave room for expansion.

notes: North America: in all four clubs read (AAA Northeast, ACSC, CAA South Central Ontario, BCAA) fuel delivery is a Basic-tier service where the member pays for the fuel and a Plus or Premier service where the fuel is free. The delivery itself uses the club's call allowance only where a source says so (CAA South Central Ontario).

Quantities: only AAA Northeast ('about 1 to 2 gallons', in its magazine, not its terms), BCAA ('up to 10 L', search summary) and Quálitas ('5 litros gratis', agent blog) give a quantity. The others say a 'limited supply' or 'sufficient' to reach the nearest station. ACSC, CAA South Central Ontario and BCAA all name a tow as the fallback, so a car can be towed instead of refuelled.

Price basis: AAA Northeast 'current pump prices'; CAA South Central Ontario 'the current pump price'; ACSC 'such service provider's applicable rates'; BCAA 'at cost'. Canadian Tire's non-member price is $90 plus tax for delivery with fuel extra.

Britain: the AA does not promise to bring fuel; its terms tow the car 'to a local fuelling station, repairer or charge point' and exclude fuel. The RAC's terms offer fuel brought to you (you pay for it), an EV charge, or a tow, whichever the patrol chooses.

EV: AAA Northeast is the only club whose terms price EV charge ($7.50 per mile of range for Basic, free for Plus and Premier). RAC gives a 10-mile boost or a 10-mile tow. The AA tows. BCAA tows within the tier's allowance or charges on the road where available. ACSC and CAA South Central Ontario say nothing.

Wait times: no club read publishes a measured average. Published figures are a target (AA 'around an hour'), a goal (AA Ireland '45-minute window') and a live estimate (CAA South Central Ontario: 30 to 47 minutes for Toronto and Peel across two small-hours reads, up to 190 for Durham specialty work).

Containers: Great Britain's Schedule 3 is the only litre limit read (10 L plastic, 20 L metal, 30 L in no more than two containers in a vehicle). The US, California and New York rules read govern the can, not the fill; they define what counts as an approved container.
